summary: A short report with a graph of how busy the BBN and USC-ISI TENEX computers were during the working week in July 1973, shown as average load by hour of the day. The author notes that reading such data is tricky and offers a few observations for the network community.

eli5.summary: It is a chart showing when two big computers were busiest during the day, like a graph of when a shop is crowded.

questions: how busy were arpanet hosts in 1973
how does computer load vary during the day
subtitle: Measuring how busy two TENEX systems were during working hours in 1973.

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed to understand how heavily used the BBN and ISI TENEX systems were at different times of day.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents hourly load average data gathered from TENEX systems for the month of July 1973, showing how computational demand varied throughout the day.
tldr.outcome: The analysis revealed that load patterns closely followed typical business hours and the time zones of users, with peaks during afternoon work periods and dips during breaks, suggesting that network usage is fundamentally tied to human work schedules.

facts.label: Time period
facts.value: Weekday hourly load averages for July 1973

today: RFC 546 is an early example of network measurement and capacity planning. While the specific data is from 1973, the principle it demonstrates—that network and system utilization follows human work patterns—remains relevant to capacity planning today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC presents utilization data for two major TENEX time-sharing systems: one at BBN (Bolt, Beranek, and Newman) and another at USC-ISI (USC Information Sciences Institute). The data measures how heavily loaded these systems were during the working week of July 1973. The TENEX load average is a measure of CPU demand, calculated as an average of the number of runnable processes over a given time period.
sections.eli5: This document shows how busy two big computers were at different times of the day in July 1973. A higher number means more people were using the computer at the same time.

sections.title: What the Data Shows
sections.content: The data reveals striking patterns in how the two systems were used. Both BBN and ISI show similar curves that begin to increase around 7-8 a.m. EDT as users begin their computing work. The load dips between 10-11 a.m. EDT when users take coffee breaks. After lunch, the load peaks sharply between 1-2 p.m. EDT as users return to work. The systems see reduced demand in the late afternoon as users leave for the day, with a local minimum around 6-7 p.m. during dinner time, followed by a second peak between 9-10 p.m. EDT when some users resume computing after dinner.
sections.eli5: The computers got busier as the morning went on, took a little break for coffee around 10 a.m., then got very busy after lunch. They got quieter in the evening when people ate dinner, but some people came back later to work again.

sections.title: Observations About the Two Sites
sections.content: The ISI system showed a smoother curve than the BBN system, with the coffee break dip appearing only as a decrease in slope rather than a sharp dip, and the dinner break being completely smoothed out. This difference is likely because ISI's users were on the West Coast and therefore operated on a different time schedule, blending their activity patterns into the overall curve. During July, the BBN system was more heavily loaded overall than ISI, though the data collected did not include the number of active jobs, making it impossible to determine whether BBN had more users or simply more demanding user jobs.
sections.eli5: The ISI computer's busy times looked smoother because people there were in a different time zone, so their work schedule mixed in with the other users. The BBN computer was busier overall, but no one knows if that was because more people used it or because the people there ran more demanding programs.
